cases.title: What 95% confidence means
cases.context: Ten resting heart rates give a sample mean of 67 beats/min, and the 95% confidence interval for the population mean is 60.56224 to 73.43776 beats/min. What does the 95% describe?
tasks: Say which quantity is fixed and which one changes from sample to sample.
Say where the cutoff comes from and what the confidence level describes in the long run.
cases.conclusion: The 95% describes the procedure. About 95 out of 100 intervals built this way contain the fixed population mean, so this one interval from 60.56224 to 73.43776 beats/min either contains it or it does not.

steps.title: Name the confidence level
steps.words: The confidence level comes from alpha. With alpha equal to 0.05 the level is 95 percent.

steps.title: The population mean is fixed
steps.words: The population mean is one fixed number that we do not know. The sample mean changes from sample to sample, so it is the interval that moves, not the population mean.

steps.title: Where the cutoff comes from
steps.words: The middle 95 percent of the t distribution lies between the negative and the positive cutoff. The other 5 percent is split into 2.5 percent in each tail, so the combined two-tail 0.05 column is used.

steps.title: Build the interval
general: \bar x-t_\alpha(\nu)\cdot s_{\bar x}<\mu<\bar x+t_\alpha(\nu)\cdot s_{\bar x}
steps.words: The interval reaches one margin below and one margin above the sample mean.

steps.title: Long-run coverage
steps.words: Before the data are collected, the procedure has a 95 percent chance of producing an interval that contains the population mean. After the data are in, this one interval either contains it or it does not.

cases.title: Deciding with a confidence interval
cases.context: The 95% confidence interval for diuretic minus placebo urine production is 31.18917 to 408.8108 mL/day. Do the population means differ at the matching two-sided 0.05 level?
tasks: State both hypotheses for the difference.
Use only the interval to decide, and give the direction.

hypotheses.nullWords: The diuretic and placebo populations have equal means.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The diuretic and placebo population means differ.

cases.conclusion: Zero is outside the interval from 31.18917 to 408.8108 mL/day, so the equal-means null is rejected at the 0.05 level. Both bounds are positive, so the diuretic mean is higher.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: For a difference of two means the null value is zero, because zero difference means equal population means.

steps.title: Match the levels
steps.words: A 95 percent interval matches a two-sided test at the 0.05 level. The levels have to match before the interval can be used for the decision.

steps.title: Check the null value
steps.words: Look for zero inside the interval. Here the whole interval sits above zero.

steps.title: Decide and give the direction
steps.words: Zero is outside, so the null is rejected. Both bounds are positive, so the first mean, the diuretic, is higher.

steps.title: Identify the population quantity
steps.words: The sample mean estimates the population mean. The SD describes individual measurements; the standard error describes uncertainty in their mean.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error
steps.words: Divide the sample SD by the square root of sample size. Keep the standard error available for the margin calculation.

steps.title: Choose degrees of freedom and the cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 9 and the combined two-tail 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.262. Do not halve the column probability again.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error

steps.words: The margin has the same measurement units as the sample mean.

steps.title: Calculate the lower endpoint
steps.words: Subtract the margin from the sample mean.

steps.title: Calculate the upper endpoint
steps.words: Add the same margin to the sample mean.

steps.title: State the population interval

steps.words: The 95% interval estimates the population mean in the original measurement units. It is not an interval containing this percentage of individual measurements.

cases.title: Diuretic versus placebo urine production
cases.context: A study compares daily urine production with a diuretic and a placebo. Assume independent Normal responses with a common population variance.
tasks: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the population difference, diuretic minus placebo. Show both variance contributions, the pooled variance, SE, df, critical value, margin, and both bounds.
Using the interval alone, decide whether the means differ at the matching two-sided 0.05 level. State both hypotheses in symbols and words, and conclude in context.

hypotheses.nullWords: The diuretic and placebo populations have equal means.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The diuretic and placebo population means differ.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x_i\) (group sample mean), \(s_i\) (group sample SD), \(n_i\) (group sample size), \(s^2\) (pooled variance), \(s_d\) (SE of the difference), \(d\) (sample difference), \(\Delta\) (population difference).
cases.conclusion: The 95% CI for diuretic minus placebo is 31.18917 to 408.8108 mL/day. The population means differ, with diuretic higher.

steps.title: Define the contrast and hypotheses
steps.words: Keep the direction diuretic minus placebo throughout. The null means equal population means; the two-sided alternative means different population means.

steps.title: Calculate the observed difference
steps.words: This is the sample estimate of the population difference in mL/day.

steps.title: Square both group SDs
steps.words: Each SD is squared before pooling, giving variances in squared measurement units.

steps.title: Pool both variance contributions
steps.words: Weight each group variance by its own degrees of freedom, add the contributions, and divide by the combined degrees of freedom.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: Add the two mean-variance contributions inside the root, then take the root. This restores the original measurement units.

steps.title: Find degrees of freedom and the t cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 18 and the combined two-tail 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.101. Do not halve the column probability again.

steps.title: Calculate the margin
steps.words: Multiply the positive cutoff by the standard error of the difference.

steps.title: Calculate both bounds
general: L=(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)-t_\alpha(\nu)\cdot s_{(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)}
U=(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)+t_\alpha(\nu)\cdot s_{(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)}
steps.words: The bounds retain the diuretic minus placebo subtraction order.

steps.title: Make the decision using the interval
steps.words: Zero is outside the interval. Reject the equal-means null at the matching two-sided 0.05 level; no separate t statistic is required.

cases.context: Of 500 college-student respondents, 177 answer yes to taking a non-prescribed stimulant in the last year. Determine whether the population proportion differs from one half.
tasks: Construct a 95% CI for the population proportion. Show the estimate, standard error, cutoff, margin, and both bounds.

hypotheses.alternativeWords: The population event proportion differs from 0.5.

steps.title: Calculate the sample proportion
steps.words: Divide event count by the total number of observations.

steps.title: Calculate the proportion SE
steps.words: Subtract the proportion from one, multiply, divide by sample size, then take the square root.

steps.title: Select the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Use the infinite-df row of the course two-tail t table. For 95% confidence, the positive cutoff is 1.96.

steps.title: Calculate the margin
general: \hat p-z_\alpha\cdot s_{\hat p}<p<\hat p+z_\alpha\cdot s_{\hat p}

steps.words: Subtract the margin from the observed proportion.

steps.title: Calculate the upper bound
steps.words: Add the same margin to the observed proportion.

cases.title: Margin of error for a two-group survey difference
cases.context: Original practice example. A campus survey asks first-year and senior students whether they use a campus fitness facility at least weekly. A news summary reports the difference in percentage points "plus or minus" a margin of error. Use the Session 17 pooled-proportion standard error and the Normal cutoff.
tasks: Find both sample proportions and their difference, first-year minus senior.
Calculate the pooled standard error and the 95% margin of error \(z_{0.05}s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\).
Report the result in survey style (difference plus or minus the margin) and decide whether the difference is significant at the two-sided 0.05 level.

hypotheses.nullWords: First-year and senior students use the facility weekly in equal proportions.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The weekly-use proportions of first-year and senior students differ.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (yes answers), \(n_i\) (respondents), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the number of yes answers divided by the number of respondents in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction first-year minus senior throughout.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: The Session 17 convention pools both groups to estimate one common proportion for the standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error

steps.words: Zero lies outside the interval because the observed difference is larger than its margin of error, so reject equal proportions at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.title: Child SBP on mother and father SBP: least squares by matrix

steps.words: Ranks are C 1, D 2, A 3, B 4, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are C, D and A.
